forces: Orchestra with offstage oboe and four timpanists
question: What changes when a familiar call receives no answer?
intro: Two shepherds answer one another across the opening silence. A pastoral melody promises repose, but the idée fixe and increasingly troubled surroundings disturb it. The ending returns to the opening call with a crucial absence: the other shepherd no longer replies. Distant thunder occupies the space instead.

sections.label: Shepherds’ dialogue
sections.mNote: Cor anglais and distant oboe exchange calls

sections.label: Pastoral melody
sections.mNote: A broad F-major theme grows through changing accompaniments

sections.label: Memory and unease
sections.mNote: The pastoral world admits the idée fixe and agitation

sections.label: Pastoral recovery

sections.label: The unanswered call

cues.title: Two distant shepherds
cues.text: The opening dialogue belongs to cor anglais and an oboe placed at a distance. Listen to the space between their phrases. Berlioz’s programme calls them shepherds; the score makes that distance a physical feature of the performance, not merely a poetic description.
cues.evidence: Score, opening bars, marks the oboe lontano and gives the answering part to cor anglais. Report: low levels and widely spaced activity across the first minute. Instrument assignment is score-derived.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Wait for the reply
cues.text: Rather than counting a regular accompaniment, listen for a phrase and its answer. The rests make each response significant. Remember that expectation: the ending will recall the call while withholding the partner that made the opening a dialogue.
cues.evidence: Opening and closing score passages, together with Berlioz’s programme. Report shows repeated low-level gaps in the opening minute; no exact call entrance is marked here.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A difficult slow movement
cues.text: Berlioz recalled spending more than three weeks on this Adagio, abandoning and returning to it. He contrasted that labour with writing the execution march in one night. The apparent ease of a pastoral scene need not reflect ease of composition.
cues.evidence: Berlioz, Memoirs, chapter 26, on composing the Adagio and march.

cues.title: A melody replaces the calls
cues.text: The movement opens out into a broader pastoral song. In the score, flute and first violins carry the principal melody over a restrained accompaniment. Listen for the difference between this continuous line and the separated calls that prepared it.
cues.evidence: Score, principal theme from bar 20; report supports a quieter F-major region around 1:45–2:10. The approximate location is not a bar alignment.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Quiet need not mean still
cues.text: Follow the accompaniment beneath the broad melody. Smaller moving figures can animate a pastoral texture without destroying its slow pace. Listen for the layers separately before deciding whether the music has become more restless.
cues.evidence: Score, pastoral theme and its changing accompaniments. This is a passage-level listening strategy, not an asserted entrance.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A scene that develops
cues.text: This is not a landscape held motionless for fifteen minutes. Berlioz varies the pastoral material, changes its surroundings and allows disturbances to accumulate. Remember the broad theme’s outline so that its later recovery can be heard as a return, not simply another quiet passage.
cues.evidence: Hector Berlioz Website score commentary describes the principal theme and its variations, interrupted by the central disturbance.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: After Beethoven’s countryside
cues.text: The F-major setting and pastoral subject invite comparison with Beethoven’s Sixth Symphony, which Berlioz knew and admired. Here, however, the countryside belongs inside one artist’s changing mental world. The beloved’s recurring melody prevents nature from becoming an escape from memory.
cues.evidence: Hector Berlioz Website score commentary discusses Beethoven’s Pastoral Symphony, F major and the idée fixe in movement III.

cues.title: A broad line, uneven strength
cues.text: Follow the shape of the phrases rather than expecting one unbroken crescendo. The pastoral material moves through stronger and quieter spans. Those small changes let unease enter without immediately replacing the scene with an obvious storm.
cues.evidence: Report: levels fluctuate between roughly −14 and −24 dB across 4:35–5:00. The cue describes the measured alternation, not a particular orchestral entrance.

cues.title: A stronger crest
cues.text: The sound reaches a stronger crest before pulling back. Compare the scale of this passage with the exposed opening calls: the same movement can move from an intimate exchange to a much fuller pressure without changing its basic slow pace.
cues.evidence: Report: 5:10–5:30 forms a strong region, including −9.5 dB at 5:25; the level falls to about −40 dB at 5:45–5:50.

cues.title: The idée fixe intrudes
cues.text: The middle of the movement admits the beloved’s melody into the pastoral scene. It is not the ball’s graceful interruption: the surrounding music makes recognition troubling. Listen for a remembered contour inside the changing texture, rather than expecting the first movement’s full presentation unchanged.
cues.evidence: Score commentary identifies the central idée fixe at bars 87–102, with altered bass material. The report’s change after the quiet 5:45–5:50 region and later 6:34–6:48 boundaries provide only an approximate middle-region placement.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Hope becomes a question
cues.text: In the programme, the artist wonders whether the beloved might betray him. Berlioz supplies the question in words; the music supplies contrasts and interruptions, not a literal spoken answer. The distinction matters when listening without the printed scenario.
cues.evidence: Berlioz’s published programme, movement III, moves from hope towards the question of betrayal.

cues.title: Calm under pressure
cues.text: After a pronounced increase in force, the music withdraws again. Listen to how quickly apparent security can change. A quiet phrase after a climax need not erase the disturbance that has just passed through it.
cues.evidence: Report: the strongest region at 7:05–7:10 gives way to −23.9 dB at 7:20, followed by further changes of level.

cues.title: The pastoral surface darkens
cues.text: The central disturbance does not need the finale’s bells or heavy brass. Strings and winds can unsettle the scene through chromatic motion, overlapping lines and changing harmonic support. Attend to the tension inside the texture rather than waiting for a new instrument to announce it.
cues.evidence: Score, disturbed central passage, uses chromatic string and wind writing; the movement does not include the finale’s bell or low-brass forces. No specific chord is timed.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A space after agitation
cues.text: The sound drops sharply before a more restrained continuation. Listen through that gap for the return of the pastoral world. Recovery is not the same as forgetting: familiar material can return carrying the memory of what interrupted it.
cues.evidence: Report: −12.0 dB at 8:25 falls to −37.8 dB at 8:35; the following change peaks occur at 8:46 and 8:52.

cues.title: Movement below the surface
cues.text: The quieter continuation contains more small attacks than its gentle level might suggest. Listen below the broad melody for the accompaniment’s motion. Softness and inactivity are different things.
cues.evidence: Report: 9:05–9:30 remains around −30 to −40 dB while detected attacks reach 1.6–2.8 per second. The report does not identify which instrument produces them.

cues.title: A pastoral theme’s earlier life
cues.text: The main pastoral theme reworks music from the Gratias of Berlioz’s early Messe solennelle. That score’s rediscovery in 1991 made the connection visible. A melody can carry an earlier compositional history without requiring a listener to hear its old words underneath it.
cues.evidence: Hector Berlioz Website, score commentary, identifies the Gratias connection and the 1991 rediscovery of the Messe solennelle.

cues.title: Strength gathers again
cues.text: The recovered pastoral texture is capable of another substantial swell. Follow it across several phrases rather than treating the first increase as the destination. The movement’s calm is repeatedly made, disturbed and remade.
cues.evidence: Report: level grows from −31.6 dB at 10:25 to −9.4 dB at 10:45 before dropping again after 10:50.

cues.title: Another quiet interior
cues.text: After the swell, the music retreats into a quieter interior. Try listening for what remains active when the total sound diminishes. A change in orchestral weight may reveal a line that was less exposed a few phrases earlier.
cues.evidence: Report: the relative level falls to −31.3 dB at 11:20 and −40.3 dB at 11:25, then begins to recover.

cues.title: A return is not a reset
cues.text: The broad pastoral material belongs to the same movement as the earlier unrest. Compare its returning shape with the beginning, but also notice what surrounds it now. Musical recurrence can preserve identity while changing the listener’s expectations.
cues.evidence: Score commentary describes the pastoral theme’s varied returns and later allusions to the idée fixe. No single recurrence is pinned to this second.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Rewritten after the premiere
cues.text: Berlioz recalled that the pastoral movement made little impression at the first performance. He later rewrote it, taking advice from Ferdinand Hiller. The scene’s carefully managed distances and silences belong to a history of revision, not to an untested first draft.
cues.evidence: Berlioz, Memoirs, chapter 31, on the pastoral movement’s reception and revision with Hiller’s advice.

cues.title: Listen through the near-silence
cues.text: A deep withdrawal opens space before the final episode. Do not mistake the reduced sound for the end of the movement. The closing call will matter because the orchestra has allowed distance and waiting to become audible again.
cues.evidence: Report: −43.2 dB at 13:10 and −53.6 dB at 13:15, followed by a restrained continuation and later changes around 13:50–14:00.

cues.title: Thunder instead of an answer
cues.text: The closing episode brings back the shepherd’s call, but its partner is absent. The score sets the cor anglais against distant thunder from four timpanists. Listen for the difference between an answering melody and a low rumble that occupies the space where an answer was expected.
cues.evidence: Programme and closing score, bars 175–196. Report: strong change at 13:58 and markedly lower brightness around 14:00–14:05 support the approximate thunder region, not instrument identification.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The programme leaves a silence
cues.text: Berlioz’s description ends this scene with solitude and silence. It does not explain away the missing response. The story works through a changed relationship between sounds: one voice remains, and a dialogue has become a call into distance.
cues.evidence: Berlioz’s published programme, final sentences of movement III, specifies the unanswered shepherd, distant thunder, solitude and silence.

cues.title: Distance outlasts the melody
cues.text: Listen to the remaining low sound and its decay rather than waiting for a final orchestral declaration. The end withdraws from the listener. Its scale is the opposite of the execution march that follows.
cues.evidence: Closing score, diminishing timpani and sustained string ending; report shows low-brightness windows around 15:15–15:20 and increasingly quiet levels thereafter.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The dream changes scene
cues.text: This silence closes the pastoral movement, not the symphony. Next comes the march to the scaffold. Keep the idée fixe in memory: there it will survive only as a brief recollection before an interruption that the programme makes fatal.
cues.evidence: Berlioz’s programme, movements III and IV, and the brief idée fixe near the march’s ending.

transitions.title: Dialogue becomes a continuous line
transitions.how: The isolated calls prepare a broader melody with accompaniment. Instead of waiting for one exposed voice to answer another, the listener can follow a sustained line. The pastoral world gains continuity without losing its restrained scale.
transitions.evidence: Score, principal theme from bar 20; report supports the quieter F-major passage around 1:45–2:10. Approximate score-based division.

transitions.title: Memory enters the landscape
transitions.how: A pronounced withdrawal opens onto the central region of recollection and disturbance. The idée fixe belongs to the same symphony, but it does not belong comfortably to this attempted pastoral repose. Familiar material becomes a source of unease.
transitions.evidence: Score, central idée fixe and surrounding disturbance; report withdrawal at 5:45–5:50 and renewed activity from 5:55. The division marks the broad approach, not the exact thematic entrance.

transitions.title: The pastoral world returns
transitions.how: The central agitation subsides, making room for the pastoral material and its altered accompaniment. A quieter texture separates the recovery from the disturbance, while the remembered theme links it to the movement’s earlier world.
transitions.evidence: Score, varied pastoral return; report level drop at 8:30–8:40 and structural changes at 8:46–8:52.

transitions.title: The opening loses its answer
transitions.how: The larger pastoral texture withdraws towards the exposed call heard at the beginning. Its former partner does not return. Low timpani rolls supply distance and threat, but no answering melody: recurrence now reveals an absence.
transitions.evidence: Score and programme, closing shepherd-and-thunder episode. Report changes at 13:50 and 13:58, with a lower-frequency region from about 14:00. Placement is approximate.

composer.epithet: He made orchestral colour, the position of a sound in space, and the return of a remembered melody into structural events.
facts: Flute and guitar as a boy; Paris Conservatoire with Jean-François Le Sueur and Anton Reicha
Critic for the Journal des débats; Conservatoire librarian; touring conductor
Shakespeare, Goethe and Virgil supplied the subjects of his largest works
Four symphonies; operas; dramatic and sacred choral works; songs; an orchestration treatise
composer.background:
Berlioz grew up in La Côte-Saint-André, between Lyon and Grenoble, in the household of a physician who taught him Latin and expected him to study medicine. He learned flute and guitar, but never acquired the pianist’s routine of composing at a keyboard. Virgil’s account of Dido’s death affected him as a schoolboy; forty years later he would set it in Les Troyens. Sent to Paris in 1821, he attended anatomy lectures while spending his evenings at the Opéra. The theatre’s performances of Gluck offered a different education: declamation, orchestral gesture and the pacing of a dramatic scene.

He abandoned medicine, studied with Jean-François Le Sueur and entered the Conservatoire in 1826. His first large works included a Messe solennelle and the unfinished opera Les Francs-juges, whose overture survived independently. The Prix de Rome required a prescribed cantata; Berlioz finally won it in 1830, on his fourth attempt. The prize sent him to the Villa Medici, but the decisive musical experiences had already happened in Paris. Conservatoire performances under François-Antoine Habeneck introduced him to Beethoven’s symphonies, while an English theatrical company introduced him to Shakespeare.
